> **Key takeaways**
> - Ask every family for an honest review, at a natural moment, with one direct link.
> - Never pay, reward or pressure anyone for a review, and never write a fake one.
> - Reply to every review in a few calm lines, and keep children's details out of it.

## Why reviews matter to parents choosing a class

A parent picking a class is trusting you with their child. Your photos and description say what you offer. Reviews say what it feels like from another parent's side: whether the teacher learns names, whether shy kids settle in, whether class starts on time.

A profile with no reviews leaves a parent guessing, and a guessing parent often keeps scrolling. Reviews are one part of being easy to trust, alongside clear details and real photos (more in [how to get more students for your kids' classes](/blog/how-to-get-more-students-for-kids-classes)).

## When to ask

Ask while the good feeling is fresh:

- After a class where something clicked: a first cartwheel, a finished painting, a song played start to finish.
- At the end of a term, a camp week or a showcase.
- When a parent thanks you, or tells you their child talks about your class at home.

One honesty point: ask every family, not only the ones you expect to be happy. Picking who gets asked bends the picture, and parents notice when every review sounds the same. Our guide to [Google Business Profile for kids' activity businesses](/blog/google-business-profile-for-kids-activity-businesses) covers Google's own review rules, including this one.

## How to ask, without pressure

### In person

Keep it short and easy to say no to:

"We're a small studio, and reviews really help other parents find us. If you have a minute this week, an honest review would mean a lot. Good or not so good, I read every one."

Then let it go. Don't hand a parent your phone at pickup, and don't wait while they type.

### By message

Send the same short note to every family:

"Hi [parent's name], thank you for bringing [child's first name] this term. If you have two minutes, we'd love an honest review of the class here: [link]. It helps other families decide if we're a good fit. Thanks either way!"

Send it once. One friendly reminder a week later is fine. A string of nudges is not.

## Make it easy

Every extra step loses a review. Cut the steps:

- Use one direct link that opens the review form, not your home page.
- Put that link in your end-of-term message, your email signature and on a small card by the door.
- Say how short it can be: "Two sentences is plenty."
- Offer a prompt without telling them what to say: "What did your child enjoy? What should a new family know?"

## The honesty rule: no paying, no rewards, no fakes

Never pay for a review, and never trade one for a reward: no discount, no gift, no extra session, no prize draw. Never write reviews yourself, and never ask friends, relatives or staff to post as if they were customers.

Fake reviews are not allowed, and many review sites, Google among them, don't allow rewards for reviews. Parents trust reviews because they are honest. A few real three- and four-star reviews beat a wall of five-star ones nobody believes.

## How to reply to reviews

Reply to every review, good or critical, within a few days. Parents read replies closely: they show how you treat people.

Some rules for every reply:

- Keep it short: two to four sentences.
- Never name a child, and never share anything about a child, a family or a booking in public.
- Stay calm. Don't argue, don't correct a parent's memory in public, and don't guess who wrote a review.
- Sound like you. A reply that reads like a form letter cools a warm review.

### Replying to a positive review

Mention one detail from their review, so it is clearly a real reply. A template:

"Thank you so much for this! We loved having you in class this term, and it's great to hear [one detail from their review]. See you next week."

### Replying to a critical review

Read it twice, then wait an hour before you answer. Then:

1. Thank them for taking the time.
2. Acknowledge the concern without arguing about the details.
3. Say what you are changing, if anything.
4. Offer to talk privately.

A template:

"Thank you for telling us about this. We're sorry the class didn't feel right, and we take it seriously. We're [what you're changing, for example: adding a five-minute welcome for new kids]. We'd like to hear more, so please message us directly any time."

Leave out what happened in class and anything a parent told you privately. A public back-and-forth only makes the review more visible. If a review breaks a site's rules (for example, it's about a different business), use that site's reporting tool instead of arguing in the reply.

## Turn feedback into improvements

Every few weeks, read recent reviews together and look for patterns:

- **The same praise again and again?** That's your strength. Use those words in your class description.
- **The same complaint twice or more?** That's a fix. Parking, a slow start to class, how you share updates with parents: small changes often clear it up.
- **A one-off complaint?** Note it and watch for it, but don't rebuild your class around one comment.

When you change something because of feedback, say so in your next term message: "You told us pickup felt rushed, so we now end five minutes earlier." Families notice when they've been heard.

## How ORYN Quest fits

## FAQ

### How do I get reviews for a kids class without being pushy?

Ask every family once, at a natural moment such as the end of a term, with one direct link. Make clear that any honest review is welcome, and don't wait while they write it.

### Can I offer a discount or a small gift for a review?

No. Never pay or reward anyone for a review, and never write fake ones. Fake reviews are not allowed, and many review sites, Google among them, don't allow rewards for reviews.

### Should I reply to every review?

Yes, good and critical, within a few days. Keep it to a few calm sentences, and never share details about a child or a family.

### What should I do about an unfair critical review?

Wait before you reply. Thank them, acknowledge the concern without arguing, say what you're changing, and offer to talk privately. If it breaks the site's rules, report it through that site.
